part_title: Deep Learning and Neural Networks Explained Visually
review_basis: Original AIF Module 03 WebP slides 01–08 personally reviewed; each narrative follows visible flow, labels and worked examples.

scenes.title: What is Deep Learning (DL)?
scenes.narration: Deep learning is a subset of machine learning that uses neural networks containing multiple layers of connected processing units. The slide contrasts traditional machine-learning methods with deep learning. Traditional methods can work very well on structured data, such as a table of sales, prices and dates, and may rely on features that people design. A feature is a measurable characteristic used to make a prediction. Deep networks can learn useful features directly from more complex inputs, including images, speech and language. Follow the central network diagram from its input layer on the left, through several hidden layers, to the output on the right. Each circle is a computational unit, not a literal brain cell. The connections carry numbers that influence how information is transformed. During training, the network adjusts these numerical parameters to reduce a chosen error measure. Multiple layers can combine simple patterns into more complicated representations. For an image, an early layer might respond to edges while later layers may detect combinations forming a shape. On the right are example uses: object detection and image classification, along with text classification, translation and language generation. The lower bar mentions GPUs, graphics processing units. They can perform many calculations in parallel, making them useful for demanding deep-learning training. A GPU is not required for every inference or every small model. Deep learning also needs appropriate data and evaluation; a complicated network does not automatically beat a simpler method. A beginner decision: for a small table predicting monthly expenses, start by considering a simpler machine-learning method. For recognizing complex visual patterns in large collections of images, deep learning may offer advantages. Choose complexity only when the task and evidence justify it.

scenes.title: Neural Networks – how do they work?
scenes.narration: Let's trace one photo through a neural network. On the left is a cat. A computer does not initially see the word 'cat'; it receives numeric pixel values representing the image. Those numbers go into the input layer, drawn as blue nodes. The middle has several hidden layers, shown with purple nodes connected by many lines. The connections have weights, which are numbers controlling how strongly one unit influences another. Inside a node, incoming values are combined, adjusted and passed through a mathematical function. The simplified panel on the right says it passes a signal when strong enough. In real neural networks, activation functions can produce many different numeric outputs, not merely an on/off decision. During training, the network sees many labeled examples and adjusts its weights to improve predictions. A useful high-level analogy is learning to recognize handwriting. At first you notice strokes and curves; later you combine them to recognize full letters. Hidden layers can learn progressively more complex relationships in a similar mathematical way. At the output, this example considers categories cat, dog and bird. The system produces scores or probabilities for those categories and chooses a prediction according to its configuration. The slide shows cat, but even a confident score can be wrong, especially if the image is blurry or the animal looks unusual. The bottom four boxes summarize connected layers, learning from examples, finding features and handling complex tasks. What happens during inference? The trained network uses its existing weights to process a new image. It does not need a person to explicitly write 'if it has whiskers, output cat' for every pattern. But training quality, safety and testing still matter.

scenes.title: Deep Learning Example
scenes.narration: This worked example shows how a deep-learning system can recognize a handwritten digit. Begin at the left with a white handwritten seven on a dark square grid. The picture is converted into numbers representing pixel brightness. That grid becomes the input to a neural network. Follow the arrows through the first hidden layer. Its illustrated features include simple strokes such as vertical, horizontal and diagonal lines. A later layer combines simple patterns into corners, curves and other structures. Higher layers can recognize combinations that resemble entire digit shapes. These are conceptual illustrations of feature learning, not a guarantee that every individual neuron behaves like a human drawing tool. On the right, the output panel lists ten possible digits from zero to nine. The highlighted row is seven. The model may produce scores that are converted into probabilities; the highest value can identify its predicted category. This is classification, not a numeric regression just because the labels happen to be digits. The model is choosing among categories called zero, one, two and so on, not estimating a continuous number. Think of a postal service reading handwritten ZIP codes or a school digitizing marks from carefully controlled forms. Such applications still require tests for messy handwriting, unusual writing styles and incorrect recognition. The example teaches four stages: input pixels, feature learning, output scores and a final predicted digit. If the model mistakes a seven for a one, what should we do? Evaluate the input, examples and performance rather than assume the highest probability must be correct. Deep learning creates useful pattern recognition capabilities, but it does not eliminate uncertainty or the need for verification.
